title: Bread a chicken tender in flour and lay it on the rack for the fryer, gripping the coated piece as little as possible
instruction: Bread the chicken tender and put it on the rack for the fryer.
context: Breading is a basic home-cooking technique for chicken tenders and cutlets, fish fillets, pork chops and tofu: each wet piece is pressed and turned in seasoned flour ("Coat fish on both sides with flour, pressing down firmly so it adheres", RecipeTin Eats; "dust each piece with flour", PBS Food, Pan-Fried Tofu). Chicken is the everyday case: "three-quarters (75%) of Americans who eat any chicken say they prepare chicken at home at least once a week" (National Chicken Council consumer survey, 2020), and recipes bread each piece by "turning to thoroughly coat and pressing to adhere. Transfer to prepared rack" (America's Test Kitchen, One-Batch Fried Chicken). The coat also comes off on fingers, so a breaded piece is handled as little as possible. Raw chicken is not practical on a shared rig, so the real trial breads a non-perishable stand-in matched to the raw tender's size, mass and wet, smooth surface: a damp cellulose sponge sealed in plastic wrap and wetted.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. Three aluminum eighth-size sheet pans, each 24.4 x 16.8 x 2.5 cm (9.6 x 6.6 x 1 in.), stand side by side with their long sides along x, all centered at x 28.0: (1) Wet pan, centered at y 19.5, holding the tender, wet and drained (no liquid left in the pan): the next piece of a batch, which recipes bread one or two pieces at a time. It lies flat on the pan's floor, long side along x, centered at (28.0, 19.5, 0.8). In simulation it is a raw breast tenderloin, 50 g, drawn 13.5 cm tip to tip, 3.7 cm wide and 1.8 cm thick, rounded and tapering; its body is an 11.5 x 3.5 x 1.4 cm box made of three 3.8 cm parts joined by two sprung hinges across its width, so it bends and droops when held by one end. On the real rig it is the stand-in: a Scotch-Brite Multi-Purpose (Ocelo) cellulose sponge (Target 4-pack, no scrubber side, 0.6 in. thick; one of the darker colors, so flour shows on it), cut with scissors to 11.4 x 3.5 x 1.5 cm, soaked, squeezed until it stops dripping, then sealed in one tight layer of plastic wrap (up&up or Glad, Target), the ends folded flat like a parcel and pressed smooth, the tape (clear) on one long face only, and weighed on a kitchen scale: about 45 to 50 g (note the weight with the trial). Before each trial it is dipped in water with a drop of dish soap per cup (so the water films instead of beading) and shaken once, taped face down. (2) Breading pan, centered at y 0: seasoned flour (all-purpose flour with 2 % paprika by weight) spread level 1 cm deep over the whole floor, about 400 mL. (3) Rack pan, centered at y -19.5, holding an eighth-size stainless wire cooling rack, 22.0 x 14.5 cm, with 3 mm wires every 1.2 cm, its grid top 1.6 cm above the table. The three pans are 2.7 cm apart and held by a strip of non-slip shelf liner under each. Real rig only (not in the simulation), to keep flour off the shared rig: (a) flour containment: the three pans stand inside one full-size aluminum sheet pan (any 26 x 18 x 1 in. full-size rimmed sheet pan, e.g. Vollrath Wear-Ever 9002, restaurant supply; a half sheet pan, 18 x 13 in., is too small: the three pans side by side need about 22 x 9.6 in.), long side along y, centered at y 0, its near rim at x 12.5, 12.5 cm in front of the arm bases, its far rim at x 58.2, the shelf-liner strips on its floor (the small pans and rack stand a few mm higher than in simulation); it stands on a plastic painter's drop cloth (3M or Hyde, hardware store) taped flat over the table. The outer pan's 1 in. rim is no higher than the small pans' rims and lies 2.4 cm or more outside them. (b) Gripper protection: before every trial, and at once if one tears, each of the four gripper fingers gets a fresh disposable nitrile glove (up&up nitrile gloves, Target, size L). A YAM finger is about 6.8 cm wide, too wide for a glove's finger, so the finger goes into the glove's palm, pad against the palm side, until its tip reaches the glove's knuckles; the glove's five fingers are folded back flat over the finger's outer face and held, with the cuff, by two turns of ScotchBlue painter's tape round the finger body above the pad. The pad's face and tip are covered by one smooth layer of nitrile with nothing loose on the gripping side; every press and grip on the tender happens through the glove. The hand is opened fully and closed once with nothing held, to check the gloves move freely. Both arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: The score is set by the bare area of the tender's surface (122.5 cm^2: the six faces of its 11.5 x 3.5 x 1.4 cm body), read once it rests on the rack's grid (in simulation: its middle over the grid, its lowest corner from 3 mm below to 1 cm above the grid's top), let go and still (in simulation: no part moving over 1 cm/s or turning over 10 degrees/s) for 1 s. Laid down or let fall a short way onto it, it scores the same. 1.0: at most 10 cm^2 bare and no hand on it; 0.75: at most 25 cm^2; 0.5: at most 50 cm^2; 0.25: at most 85 cm^2; 0: more. A hand still on it caps the score at 0.5. Left resting in the breading pan instead, let go and still for 1 s, with at most 25 cm^2 bare: 0.25. Anywhere else at the end: 0. Fallen off the table: 0 (food off the floor is thrown away). Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Why: turning the tender and moving it usually take grips, and a grip takes the coat off under the finger pads; gripped at one spot each time, the marks stay under 10 cm^2, while every extra grip at a new spot costs the top tier. One face pressed and the other not leaves well over 50 cm^2 bare. How the simulation decides: the surface is 2.5 mm cells, bare at the start. A cell is coated where the tender is pressed into the flour, the standard technique: the pan pushing up on it several times its weight while a hand pushes it down firmly, held briefly (not the impact of a drop), read from PhysX contact forces; a press coats the cells in the flour along a stretch of the tender around where it is pushed. Lying in the flour or dropped into it coats nothing. A grip (both fingers pushing on it from opposite sides, as any pinch that can lift it does) wipes the coat under the pads' inner faces (our modeling choice). Coated cells left on the bare table off the pans rub off. Pressing a bare spot again re-coats it. Real trial: whatever coat is on the stand-in counts, pressed or not. In diffuse light, no flash, photograph its top, both long sides and both ends with a card ruled in 5 mm squares beside it (nothing touches the coat); lift the rack out by its edges and photograph the underside from below through the grid (one left in the breading pan is first lifted out by one end with tongs and laid on the rack). A square more than half bare (the wrapped sponge's color showing, no flour) is bare (0.25 cm^2 each); a square partly hidden by a wire is judged by its visible part, one fully hidden counts as bare. The video shows where it ended and that it was let go.
reset_notes: Between real trials: pull the gloves off the fingers (tape and all) and throw them away; dry-wipe the wrists, gripper bodies, finger roots and finger slides with a dry microfiber cloth, or a hand vacuum, so no flour is left on the robot, and put fresh gloves on (setup). Rinse the flour off the wrapped sponge under the tap, dip it in the soapy water, shake once and lay it flat in the wet pan as specified, taped face down. Sieve the flour to take out wet clumps, top it up and level it at 1 cm with a ruler; brush the rack clean. Sweep or vacuum spilled flour out of the outer sheet pan and off the drop cloth. Replace all the flour each session. After each session unwrap the sponge, rinse it and let it dry; at the next session soak, squeeze, re-wrap and weigh it (or cut a fresh one from the 4-pack). In simulation every trial starts with a bare tender.
fidelity: Size and mass matched, not meat: the rig breads a damp sponge sealed in plastic wrap and wetted, so flour holds only to a thin water film; unlike meat the wrap absorbs no water, and how well the coat holds (and the grip on it) compared with chicken is untested. Sim: three rigid box parts on two sprung hinges (no taper; less droop); bare pads, no gloves or outer pan; a cell is coated only by a press, wiped by a grip or the bench; a two-fist or scooped carry wipes nothing.
scores: Demo (scripted): 1.0, success at step 1,444 with 8.8 cm^2 bare (92.8 % coated). Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps).
